article_title: ICE at US airports; Congress urged to end shutdown: Live updates
article_content:
Could a deal to fund TSA be coming? Latest as ICE deployed to airports
Lawmakers desperate for a deal to fund the Transportation Security Administration said an agreement may be within reach, but it's not a done deal as the partial government shutdown and a deadly runway accident in New York further strained air travel.
The shutdown, which began in mid-February, has led to a significant increase in TSA absences as employees have worked without regular pay for over a month. Travelers have endured long wait times at security checkpoints at airports due to staffing shortages.
Since the shutdown began, federal officials said more than 400 TSA officers have resigned. In response to the growing number of callouts, President Donald Trump deployed immigration agents to major airports.
The move has raised concerns from the TSA workers' labor union, which said immigration agents have not received the months of airport security training required. Agents have been seen at over a dozen airports, including in Georgia, New York and New Jersey.
Republican lawmakers said after a Tuesday meeting with President Donald Trump that negotiations were gaining serious momentum for the first time in more than a month. But some Democrats cast doubt on the talks, saying they don't include make-or-break reforms for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Catch up with live coverage from the USA TODAY Network.
Democrats throw cold water on shutdown deal, call for more ICE reforms
Zachary Schermele
As negotiations ramp up on Capitol Hill to end the partial shutdown, Senate Democrats seem to be clinging to a particular word: reforms.
It was a term party leaders used in the context of Immigration and Customs Enforcement nearly two dozen times during a Tuesday news conference.
The refrain threw cold water on a new GOP compromise to fund the critical agency – minus ICE's enforcement and removal operations – and end a crisis that has upended air travel across the country.
"Democrats are continuing to push for modest reforms," Washington Sen. Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, told reporters. "The current Republican offer in front of us does not do that."
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-New York, said Democrats would send back a counterproposal that included more provisions to "rein in" ICE and Border Patrol. Democrats have repeatedly demanded a ban on masks for immigration enforcement agents and raids without judicial warrants, among other stipulations.
Read more here.
'They are doing God's work'
Trevor Hughes
At Denver International Airport, arriving passenger Tricia Hernandez, 27, said she was pleasantly surprised at how smooth her security experience was flying out of California.
A part-time server and college student, she expressed solidarity with TSA workers.
“I was shocked at the camaraderie and community,” Hernandez said. “They are doing God's work.”
Hernandez said she hopes the government shutdown gets resolved soon and workers start getting paid again. She said she wouldn't be taking the uncertainty with as much grace as they are: “I would probably not have such a good attitude.”
Union leader says ICE isn't helping wait times at airports
Zach Wichter
TSA union officials at a press conference on Tuesday said the ongoing shutdown continues to be a drain on their members – and ICE isn’t doing anything to alleviate the strain at airports.
Aaron Barker, president of Local 554 of the Association of Federal Government Employees, which represents TSA workers at Atlanta-Hartsfield Jackson International Airport, said ICE agents are largely patrolling lines and not doing other TSA tasks.
“Atlanta Airport already has staff that does that, they’re not TSA employees,” Barker said. “For (TSA officers) to have (ICE agents) come in knowing they’re collecting a per diem check and hotels to come to these airports while officers aren’t receiving a paycheck, it’s a waste of money that could have been coming into these officers’ bank accounts.”
A look at ICE in the Atlanta airport
Irene Wright
On the first morning ICE officers were deployed to the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, lines for security topped four hours long, with some passengers reporting waits even longer.
The officers were sent to airports to make getting through TSA lines faster, but a USA TODAY reporter's trip to the Atlanta airport on Monday yielded different observations: Most ICE officers were standing around in groups, sitting in the small food court grabbing a bite to eat or a coffee break or watching airport staff struggle to direct lines without stepping in.
Photos and videos posted by passengers on social media also show ICE officers standing behind the TSA officers while they checked identification before sending travelers through the security screening. Passengers told USA TODAY they didn't see the officers helping speed things up.
"It feels kind of like a photo op, I don't know, posturing," said Maddox Gates, an Atlanta native who now lives in New York City and was traveling home with his debate team.
Could a deal to fund TSA be close?
Zachary Schermele
There's new optimism on Capitol Hill that a deal to end the nearly six-week-long shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security may be in reach before Congress goes on spring break, potentially ending widespread airport tumult as millions of Americans gear up to travel.
Republican lawmakers emerged from a Tuesday meeting with President Donald Trump saying negotiations were gaining serious momentum for the first time in more than a month.
Sen. Katie Britt, an Alabama Republican who chairs a Senate subcommittee overseeing DHS funding, has been spearheading negotiations. After sitting down at the White House with the president, she told reporters an agreement appeared to be on the horizon and Republicans were working to solidify the details.
The tentative agreement is likely to include funding for all of DHS, including TSA, but exclude Immigration and Customs Enforcement's removal and enforcement operations, according to a person familiar with the talks.
'This is so un-American': TSA workers struggling without pay
Trevor Hughes
Angela Grana, the Colorado-based regional vice president of the union representing TSA workers at 38 airports across the Rockies, said some of her colleagues are sleeping in their cars between shifts to save gas money. She told USA TODAY that many workers saw short paychecks in February during the previous shutdown, and were still trying to catch up when their pay halted again.
"This is so un-American," said Grana. "We are living paycheck to paycheck already as the worst-paid federal employers. We're nobodies with the biggest responsibility."
Grana said many flyers don't realize how tough things are for the agents they're seeing at airports because dedicated TSA employers are putting on a brave face for the traveling public. Grana's AFGE TSA Local 1127 represents about 4,000 workers across six states, including Utah, Oregon and Montana.
"We're basically invisible and we can't let you see that our guard is down," Grana said. "But we are desperate. The anxiety is exhausting."
Former TSA official: ICE officers could deter terrorists
Jeanine Santucci
A former TSA administrator said the presence of immigration officers at airports could have benefits other than speeding up lines, including acting as a "deterrant" to would-be terrorists.
John Pistole, who headed up TSA under former President Barack Obama and also served as deputy FBI director, told CNN on Tuesday that potential terrorists could look to exploit the situation that has seen hundreds of TSA agents quit and long, winding lines of people.
"(T)hese long lines are a soft target for a putative terrorist, somebody who wants to come in and make a name for themselves, for their cause," Pistole said on CNN This Morning. "And so if the – somebody comes in, any one of these terminals around the country where we have these long lines, hundreds, thousands, perhaps, people just winding back and forth, and they see these armed officers, that may be a visible deterrent. So, that could be a good thing."
Long TSA lines delayed LaGuardia crash investigators
Jeanine Santucci
The long wait times to get through security caused delays for investigators responding to the crash scene at LaGuardia airport overnight Sunday into Monday, National Transportation Safety Board Chair Jennifer Homendy said.
NTSB investigators began arriving at the scene of the crash by 3 a.m., within hours of the crash, she said, but at least one specialist was caught up in the lines.
"We have our air traffic control specialist who was in line with TSA for three hours until we called in Houston to beg to see if we can get her through so we can get her here," Homendy said. "So it's been a really big challenge to get the entire team here."
Homendy said investigators would still be arriving through the early morning hours on Tuesday.
How to check TSA wait times at your airport
Saman Shafiq and Michelle Del Rey
Airports around the country have seen TSA lines and wait times balloon, and travelers forced to stand in long queues, some of which have stretched outside terminals.
There are several ways to check TSA wait times, though some airports are not offering real-time updates.
- Airport websites: Most airport websites, including Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport and Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport, post expected wait times to help travelers plan their trip. However, others such as New York City's JFK and Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson are not posting real-time data, instead advising travelers to "allow extra time when traveling."
- Independent websites such as Airport Insight and TSA Wait Times offer real-time information on security wait times at airports.
TSA's official website and app, MyTSA, isn’t being updated because of the ongoing government shutdown, the agency said in a statement on Feb. 17.
TSA officers say ICE agents are adding confusion
Steve Bannon: Is ICE in airports a 'test run' for elections?
Jeanine Santucci
Former Trump aide Steve Bannon suggested that the deployment of immigration agents to airports could be a "test run" for making a similar move during upcoming midterm elections.
"We can use what's happening with these ICE helping out at the airports, we can use this as a test run, as a test case to really perfect ICE's involvement in the 2026 midterm elections, sir?" Bannon asked conservative lawyer Mike Davis during an episode of his "War Room" podcast that aired Monday.
Davis responded that ICE agents should be deployed to polling locations because people who are in the country illegally can't vote, and U.S. citizens should be glad to see immigration agents there.
"Pick them out of line starting today and maybe the lines get shorter," Bannon said.
Airport leaders urge Congress to end TSA funding standoff
Reuters
More than 100 airport leaders on Monday implored Congress in a letter to end a funding standoff that has forced 50,000 Transportation Security Administration officers to go unpaid and has led to massive security lines.
The CEOs of Airports Council International — North America and American Association of Airport Executives, along with more than 100 airport leaders, urged an end to the impasse, citing concerns "about the growing operational disruptions at airports... The impacts of the shutdown are significant, growing, and potentially long-lasting."
LaGuardia Airport runway closed following crash
Thao Nguyen
Following the crash at New York's LaGuardia Airport late on Sunday, federal investigators said the runway where the incident took place will be closed for days.
The National Transportation Safety Board will lead the crash investigation, and Canadian government investigators will head to New York to participate in the probe.
"I just want to express how much debris there is," Jennifer Homendy, chair of the NTSB, said at a news conference Monday night. "We need to go through all that."
She said investigators need to photograph the crash debris and transport some materials to labs in Washington, DC. Investigators were able to recover the plane’s cockpit voice recorder, a device that records the pilots’ conversation, and the plane’s flight data recorder or black box.
Investigators began arriving at the scene at 3 a.m. local time, within hours of the crash, according to Homendy. The Transportation Security Administration shutdown delayed the arrival of some investigators, she suggested.
Contributing: Michael Loria, USA TODAY
ICE agents deployed to over a dozen airports
Thao Nguyen
Federal immigration agents were deployed at more than a dozen airports across the United States on Monday amid the Transportation Security Administration staffing issues. The Department of Homeland Security confirmed that it sent hundreds of immigration agents to assist with airport security.
While Tom Homan, the White House border czar, said immigration agents were being sent to airports with the longest wait lines, he did not disclose which airports — citing potential risk of protests.
Federal officers were being deployed to airports in Atlanta, New York City, Newark, New Jersey, New Orleans, Cleveland, Pittsburgh, Phoenix, and Fort Myers, Florida, according to local officials and social media posts. Both The New York Times and CNN reported that agents were being sent to 14 airports. Read more here.
